basic_info.name: SMART on FHIR JavaScript client (smart-on-fhir/client-js; npm package 'fhirclient')
basic_info.description: This is the reference JavaScript/TypeScript client library for connecting SMART-on-FHIR apps to FHIR servers in the browser and in Node.js. It handles the SMART App Launch OAuth2 flow (EHR launch and standalone launch), token acquisition and refresh, PKCE and asymmetric client authentication, discovery via .well-known/smart-configuration (falling back to /metadata), and then exposes a FHIR REST client (client.request plus create/update/delete/patch and patient/user/encounter context helpers) that returns parsed FHIR JSON. The single most load-bearing fact for this sweep is its maintenance status: it is alive but essentially stalled - the newest stable release is v2.6.3 (2025-09-26), a 3.0.0-beta line exists (3.0.0-beta.2, 2025-09-29), and the last commit to the default branch was 2025-12-22, meaning there has been no repository or release activity during the last six months. It is Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file: 'Copyright 2015 Boston Children's Hospital'), maintained under the SMART Health IT / Boston Children's Hospital umbrella by a small number of individuals (notably vlad-ignatov), and the GitHub repository is itself a fork of jmandel/fhir-js-client. For MediKiosk Module C it is relevant only to the physician-screen / HIS-side integration surface - SMART launch and FHIR REST transport - and is not designed for offline-first operation, since OAuth2 launch and FHIR reads require connectivity.
basic_info.organization: smart-on-fhir organisation / SMART Health IT, hosted at Boston Children's Hospital (Josh Mandel's group lineage; the repo is a fork of jmandel/fhir-js-client). Maintained by a small set of individuals, principally Vladimir Ignatov (vlad-ignatov), with contributing maintainers including dtphelan1 and smarthealthit-chip. The npm maintainer list is dtphelan1 and smarthealthit-chip.
basic_info.country: United States (Boston Children's Hospital / SMART Health IT, Boston, MA). The library is used internationally and is not India-specific.
basic_info.status: Production/stable but dormant-to-low-velocity. No deprecation notice and the repository is not archived; it is widely deployed historically. However, there have been no releases and no commits since December 2025, so within the last six months the project has been inactive. A 3.0.0 beta exists but has not progressed to stable.

technical_features.what_it_does: The library implements the client half of SMART on FHIR and generic FHIR REST access. Its SMART API exposes authorize(options) to begin the OAuth2 launch (supporting EHR launch with iss/launch parameters and standalone launch, multiple launch configurations via issMatch, and options such as client_id, scope, redirectUri, completeInTarget, noRedirect and PKCE/asymmetric authentication), ready() to complete the flow on the redirect URI and return a configured client, and an experimental init(). The returned client provides request(url, options) plus convenience create/update/delete/patch methods, patient/user/encounter context read helpers, iterate/bundle pagination, resolveReferences, includeResponse (raw Response access for headers/status), request aborting, and getFhirVersion()/getFhirRelease() introspection. It prefers .well-known/smart-configuration for discovery and falls back to the CapabilityStatement at /metadata, and can refresh tokens and use a fake/test token flow for open servers. It is purely an auth-and-transport layer: it does not generate clinical summaries, parse documents, or run terminology logic.
technical_features.architecture: Written in TypeScript and compiled to multiple targets: an IIFE browser bundle (dist/bundle/fhir-client.js and .min.js, also served via jsDelivr/unpkg CDN), ESM and CJS module builds (dist/esm, dist/cjs), plus a Node entry point and a legacy Hapi.js entry point. Adapter layer abstracts environment differences (BrowserAdapter, NodeAdapter, HapiAdapter). Authentication uses the jose library for JWT/JWK handling; HTTP uses cross-fetch with abortcontroller-polyfill and isomorphic-webcrypto for crypto in both browser and Node. Since v2.0 the fhir.js library was removed as core and became an optional, separately included dependency. Tests use Nightwatch with headless Chrome (e2e) and lab for unit tests; builds run through webpack and babel.
technical_features.inputs: A FHIR server base URL or the SMART launch parameters (iss, launch), OAuth2 client configuration (client_id, scope, redirect URI, optional PKCE/asymmetric keys), and FHIR REST requests (resource type/search/read/create/update/delete/patch). It consumes JSON FHIR resources returned by the server. It does not ingest patient dialogue, scanned documents, audio or vitals, and has no NLP capability.
technical_features.outputs: JavaScript/TypeScript FHIR client instances, OAuth2 access/refresh tokens and authorized sessions, and parsed FHIR resources/Bundles as JSON objects (or the raw Fetch Response when includeResponse is set). It does not emit clinical summaries, Compositions or ABDM/NRCeS profiles - it moves FHIR resources to and from a server.
technical_features.standards_compliance: Implements the SMART App Launch / SMART on FHIR authorization framework and OAuth2, including PKCE (since v2.5.0) and asymmetric client authentication (private_key_jwt), scope handling, and SMART discovery via .well-known/smart-configuration. It speaks generic FHIR REST across DSTU2/STU3/R4 (getFhirVersion returns 2/3/4, or 0 if unknown) and works with R4 servers (the docs' canonical test server is r4.smarthealthit.org). Conformance here is protocol-level (SMART/OAuth2/FHIR REST), not clinical-profile-level: the library does not validate resources against FHIR profiles, Implementation Guides, or the NRCeS ABDM IG, does not enforce terminology bindings, and does not claim ABDM/India conformance. The v2.6.x line also added request options for the well-known and conformance endpoints. Note that ABDM/NRCeS is adopted via India's own consent/gateway APIs (HIP/HIU) rather than SMART-on-FHIR launch, so this library's compliance value for Module C is limited to SMART/SMART-compatible HIS/EHR endpoints.
technical_features.offline_capability: Weak - it is a network client by design. SMART launch is an OAuth2 authorization-code flow requiring both an authorization server and a FHIR server to be reachable; token refresh also needs the auth server. The static JavaScript bundle itself can be vendored and loaded fully offline (CDN or local file), so the library imposes no runtime network dependency beyond the endpoints it talks to, but authentication and FHIR data access do require connectivity. There is no local storage, encryption, caching or store-and-forward mechanism in the library. This makes it a poor fit for MediKiosk's offline-first kiosk path and only relevant where connectivity is present (e.g. a HIS-side or physician-screen integration inside a connected clinic network).
technical_features.languages_supported: Not a natural-language tool; it passes FHIR string content through unchanged, so Hindi/Devanagari/Hinglish values in FHIR resources are preserved as ordinary UTF-8 strings. No translation, transliteration or bilingual rendering is provided. [uncertain] Any script-specific issues are limited to JavaScript string/JSON handling.
technical_features.deployment_model: Runs wherever JavaScript runs: in the browser as a script tag/bundle or ESM/CJS module, or in Node.js (documented as Node 18+ in current docs; the v2.5.x line stated Node 14-18). It is a small client library with no GPU requirement and negligible RAM/CPU cost, so it imposes no meaningful load on a constrained kiosk or physician workstation. It requires a secure context (HTTPS) in browsers - the library throws if the app runs without one - which is a practical deployment constraint for clinic LAN setups. It is client-side code, not a server; it must be paired with a reachable SMART authorization server and FHIR endpoint.

performance_metrics.accuracy_or_quality_metrics: Not applicable in the ML sense - no accuracy/F1/ROUGE figures exist because it is a transport/auth library. Its quality signals are protocol-correctness tests (unit tests plus Nightwatch headless-browser e2e tests) and a history of CVE-driven dependency updates (npm audit fixes are recurring commits). There is no published conformance-score or error-rate metric. [uncertain] Coverage numbers were not captured.
performance_metrics.latency: No published latency or throughput figures. As a thin HTTP/OAuth wrapper, its overhead is dominated by the network round trips to the auth server and FHIR endpoint rather than by the library itself. [uncertain] No measured figures.
performance_metrics.resource_requirements: Minimal: a browser or Node.js runtime plus a handful of small dependencies (jose, debug, core-js, js-base64, cross-fetch, isomorphic-webcrypto, abortcontroller-polyfill). No GPU, no significant RAM or storage footprint, so it is unproblematic on a ~4GB CPU/iGPU kiosk or on a physician terminal in terms of resource cost - the constraint is connectivity and HTTPS, not resources. Peer dependencies on @types/hapi and @types/node are optional/type-only.
performance_metrics.scale_metrics: At verification: 354 GitHub stars, 221 forks, 29 watchers, 30 open issues and 801 commits; the package is listed with maintainers dtphelan1 and smarthealthit-chip on npm. Precise npm weekly-download counts were not captured. Historically it is one of the most widely referenced SMART-on-FHIR JS clients (it underpins many EHR-embedded apps and SMART Health IT sandboxes), but growth has flattened with the release cadence. [uncertain] download volume.
performance_metrics.evaluation_protocol: No clinical or human evaluation, and none is applicable. Quality assurance is engineering-based: unit tests (lab) and end-to-end browser tests (Nightwatch/headless Chrome) run in GitHub Actions, with build/docs regeneration per release, and continuous dependency/CVE remediation. The meaningful test for MediKiosk would be a functional SMART launch against the specific HIS/EHR FHIR endpoint being integrated - if that endpoint is SMART-compatible at all.

milestone_significance.relevance_to_module_c: Module C produces a structured OPConsultRecord for the physician and ABDM; this library does not help produce or validate that summary. Its relevance is narrow but real on the integration edges: if MediKiosk ever embeds as a SMART app inside a physician's EHR/HIS, or needs to launch against a SMART-compatible FHIR endpoint to pull prior context or push the attested summary, this is the canonical JavaScript client for that launch and REST access - convenient for a JS/Node physician-screen tier. It is also a useful reference implementation of SMART launch security (PKCE, asymmetric auth, discovery, token refresh) that Module C's HIS-side integration can mirror. But it is a poor fit for the offline-first, air-gapped kiosk itself, because SMART/OAuth2 and FHIR reads require connectivity, and it offers nothing for elicitation, document digitisation, AYUSH content, bilingual summarisation or NRCeS profile conformance. Treat it as optional HIS-side plumbing, not as a Module C dependency.
milestone_significance.what_to_adopt_or_reject: Adopt (conditionally): (1) the library as the SMART launch + FHIR REST transport if and only if a target HIS/EHR exposes a SMART-on-FHIR endpoint and the deployment has connectivity; (2) its security patterns as a reference for any OAuth2 integration Module C builds (PKCE, private_key_jwt, .well-known/smart-configuration discovery, expiry-aware token refresh rather than reacting to 401s); (3) its includeResponse/HttpError handling approach for reading OperationOutcome bodies on failure, which is useful when ABDM/FHIR servers reject a submission. Reject or adapt: (1) do NOT place it on the offline kiosk critical path - it cannot operate without network; (2) do NOT assume SMART covers ABDM - the ABDM gateway uses consent-manager-based HIP/HIU flows, not SMART launch, so a SMART client does not deliver ABDM integration; (3) do NOT rely on it for validation or summarisation; (4) given the stalled maintenance, pin an exact version (2.6.3) and vendor the built bundle locally rather than pulling '@latest', and be ready to fork/patch security-sensitive dependencies yourself.
milestone_significance.limitations_and_risks: Primary risk is maintenance dormancy: no release since v2.6.3 (2025-09-26) and no commit since 2025-12-22, with a 3.0.0 beta abandoned mid-stream, so security fixes depend on a small volunteer team; this matters because the library handles OAuth tokens and JWT/JWK material. Second, it is network-bound and secure-context-bound (HTTPS), which conflicts with MediKiosk's offline-first kiosk premise and can be awkward on a clinic LAN without TLS. Third, it has no relationship to ABDM/NRCeS: it cannot launch against the ABDM gateway's consent-based flows, does not know NRCeS profiles, and will not validate an OPConsultRecord. Fourth, protocol scope: the getFhirVersion mapping documents DSTU2/STU3/R4 but not R5, so R5-only servers are effectively unsupported. Fifth, licence-scanning nuance - although npm and the README declare Apache-2.0 and the LICENSE file carries a Boston Children's Hospital Apache-2.0 notice, GitHub's licensee reports NOASSERTION/Other because the file is an abbreviated notice rather than the full licence text, which could trip automated compliance gates. Sixth, the repository being a fork can confuse contribution/version provenance. None of these are blocking for an optional HIS-side integration, but they argue against making it architectural.
milestone_significance.differentiator_vs_medikiosk: It is not a competitor and it does not touch MediKiosk's core differentiation. It neither emits NRCeS-conformant summaries, nor handles offline operation, India data residency, per-field provenance, AYUSH content, bilingual output or physician attestation; it simply carries FHIR/OAuth traffic. On the integration axis it is mildly complementary: it could help MediKiosk hand the signed summary to a SMART-capable HIS, but it cannot substitute for the ABDM-specific gateway integration or for Module C's conformance machinery. If anything, its dormancy and its SMART/ABDM mismatch reinforce why MediKiosk should keep its differentiators in the elicitation-to-summary and NRCeS-emission layers rather than depending on general-purpose JS FHIR clients.

business_info.license: Apache License 2.0 (Apache-2.0). The repository LICENSE file states 'Copyright 2015 Boston Children's Hospital' and references Apache-2.0; the README says 'Apache 2.0'; and npm metadata records license 'Apache-2.0'. Caveat: GitHub's automated licensee reports the repository licence as NOASSERTION/Other because the LICENSE file is an abbreviated Apache-2.0 notice rather than the full licence text, so a formal SPDX scan should confirm it manually.
business_info.pricing: Free and open source (npm i fhirclient). No paid tier or commercial licence; no commercial support offering.
business_info.funding: Developed and hosted within the academic/non-profit SMART Health IT effort at Boston Children's Hospital, historically supported by US federal health-IT grant funding (e.g. ONC-funded SMART and FHIR projects). No venture funding and no commercial backing specific to this repository were found. [uncertain] Current-year funding status is not documented on the repository.
business_info.commercial_status: Free community/academic open-source project (unpaid), maintained by a small group under Boston Children's Hospital's SMART Health IT programme rather than by a commercial vendor.

competition_ecosystem.competitors: Other SMART/FHIR client libraries: the official smart-on-fhir Python client, fhirclient (Python), the HAPI FHIR client (Java), the Firely .NET SDK client, fhir-kit-client and the FHIR JavaScript clients (Node), ashlar/angular-fhir for front-end frameworks, and generic OAuth2 + fetch/REST stacks built in-house. For ABDM specifically, the relevant alternatives are not SMART clients at all but ABDM gateway SDKs (e.g. the NHA/ABDM sandbox tooling and the ABDM Health Data Management Policy-aligned PSP tooling and, in the wider Indian ecosystem, projects such as the Nirmitee/AMRIT-style ABDM FHIR helpers). For pure FHIR REST without SMART, plain fetch/axios plus a resource model library is the low-dependency alternative.
competition_ecosystem.integrations: Integrates with any SMART-on-FHIR compliant FHIR endpoint and any FHIR R4 server for REST operations (the project's own sandbox is r4.smarthealthit.org), and it is commonly used by EHR-embedded SMART apps and by the SMART Health IT reference/sandbox infrastructure. In Node it integrates with the Hapi.js framework via a dedicated adapter. It has no native integration with the ABDM gateway roles (HIP/HIU/PHR), health lockers, Indian HIS/EMR vendors, or AYUSH systems, and does not integrate with NRCeS profiles or NAMASTE terminology. Any ABDM integration must be built separately.
competition_ecosystem.ecosystem_notes: SMART on FHIR is a mature international standard stack driven by Boston Children's Hospital's SMART Health IT programme and HL7, but the JavaScript client's declining cadence is a mild ecosystem signal - the center of gravity for maintained FHIR tooling has shifted toward server-side and typed-generator stacks, and to India-specific ABDM tooling for the Indian market. For MediKiosk, the decisive ecosystem fact is structural: ABDM's consent-based HIP/HIU data exchange is not SMART-on-FHIR launch, so Indian ABDM integrations use ABDM gateway APIs rather than SMART clients. SMART remains useful only when targeting international or SMART-enabled HIS/EHR products. There is no government programme, NRCeS guidance, or ABDM endorsement that makes this library part of the Indian compliance path.

history.release_date: The repository was created on GitHub on 2014-05-28 (as a fork lineage of jmandel/fhir-js-client); the SMART on FHIR JS client has been published since the mid-2010s, with v1.x and then a major v2 rewrite in TypeScript (early 2020).
history.key_milestones: 2014-05-28 repository created. v1.x era (fhir.js bundling, IE-era browser support). v2.0 (2020) rewritten in TypeScript, fhir.js made optional, ES modules support. v2.3-2.4 added includeResponse, HttpError.response, patch, getState, path operator. v2.5.0 (2022-08) added PKCE and asymmetric client authentication, dropped IE10, preferred .well-known/smart-configuration, added GitHub Actions and headless-browser e2e tests. v2.5.3 (2024-02), v2.5.4 (2024-08), v2.5.5 (2025-02, refreshTokenWithClientId and user-defined state key). v2.6.0 (2025-05) added the FhirClient base class for open servers and made @types/hapi optional; v2.6.1/2.6.2 (2025-09-19) added wellKnownRequestOptions/conformanceRequestOptions and typing/test improvements; v2.6.3 (2025-09-26) fixed authorization headers on sub-request methods; 3.0.0-beta.1 and beta.2 (2025-09-25/29) published but not promoted to stable.
history.recent_changes_last_6_months: None. The last release was v2.6.3 on 2025-09-26 and the last commit to the default branch was 2025-12-22 (an npm audit dependency fix and a .gitignore update). Throughout the Mar-Sep 2026 window the repository had no commits, no releases, and no progress on the 3.0.0 beta; GitHub reports pushed_at 2025-12-22. This is the key currency finding for the sweep: the library is not abandoned or deprecated, but it is dormant, and any adoption should assume self-supported dependency maintenance.

market_positioning.target_users: Front-end and Node.js developers building SMART-on-FHIR applications - especially EHR-embedded apps, patient-facing portals, and health-app integrators connecting to SMART-enabled FHIR servers. Also used by the SMART Health IT sandbox/reference ecosystem and by HIS/EHR vendors exposing SMART endpoints. It is a developer library, not a clinician- or patient-facing product.
market_positioning.market_segment: SMART-on-FHIR / FHIR client tooling and healthcare interoperability auth-and-transport libraries - the client-side counterpart to FHIR servers and IG validators. It sits in the ambient/integration plumbing layer, not in intake, summarisation, PHR, AYUSH software, diagnostics-kiosk or benchmarking segments.
market_positioning.positioning_statement: It presents itself simply and declaratively as the 'SMART on FHIR JavaScript Library' and 'JavaScript client for FHIR' - a library for connecting SMART apps to FHIR servers that 'works both in browsers ... and on the server (NodeJS)', installed with npm i fhirclient, with documentation at docs.smarthealthit.org/client-js. Its pitch is standards-aligned SMART launch plus a simple FHIR REST client (a stated goal since v2 was to offer 'a simple alternative to fhir.js' via client.request).
